title: Book Four (1806) — Chapter 5
paragraphs: "Well, begin!" said Dolokhov.

"All right," said Pierre, still wearing the same smile. A feeling of dread hung in the air. It was clear that this affair, so casually begun, could no longer be stopped — it was taking its own course, beyond anyone's control.
Denisov went first to the barrier and announced: "As the adversaries have refused a reconciliation, please proceed. Take your pistols, and at the word three, begin to advance."
"One! Two! Three!" he shouted angrily, and stepped aside.

The two men advanced along the trampled paths, drawing closer and closer, beginning to make each other out through the mist. They were free to fire whenever they chose as they approached the barrier. Dolokhov walked slowly without raising his pistol, his bright, sparkling blue eyes fixed intently on his opponent's face. His mouth wore its usual hint of a smile.

"So I can fire whenever I want!" said Pierre, and at the word "three" he walked quickly forward, missing the trampled path and stepping into deep snow. He held the pistol in his outstretched right hand, apparently afraid of shooting himself with it. He kept his left hand carefully behind him, because he wanted to steady his right hand with it but knew he wasn't supposed to. After advancing six paces and straying off the path into the snow, Pierre glanced down at his feet, then quickly looked up at Dolokhov and, bending his finger as he'd been shown, fired. Not at all expecting such a loud report, Pierre flinched at the sound and then, smiling at his own reaction, stood still. The smoke, made denser by the mist, blocked his view for a moment, but there was no second shot as he had expected. He only heard Dolokhov's hurried steps, and then his figure emerged through the smoke. He was pressing one hand to his left side while the other clutched his drooping pistol. His face was pale. Rostov ran toward him and said something.

"N-no!" Dolokhov muttered through clenched teeth. "No, it's not over." And after stumbling a few staggering steps right up to the saber marker, he collapsed onto the snow beside it. His left hand was bloody; he wiped it on his coat and propped himself up with it. His frowning face was deathly pale and trembling.
"Plea—" Dolokhov began, but couldn't get the word out at first.
"Please," he managed with effort.
Pierre, barely holding back his sobs, started running toward Dolokhov and was about to cross the space between the barriers when Dolokhov shouted:

"Back to your barrier!" Pierre understood what was meant and stopped by his saber. Only ten paces separated them. Dolokhov lowered his head to the snow and bit at it hungrily, then raised his head again, adjusted his position, drew in his legs, and sat up, searching for a firm center of gravity. He sucked and swallowed the cold snow; his lips quivered, but his eyes, still smiling, glittered with effort and fury as he summoned his remaining strength. He raised his pistol and took aim.
"Sideways! Shield yourself with your pistol!" shouted Nesvitski.
"Take cover!" even Denisov cried out to his opponent.

Pierre, with a gentle smile of pity and remorse, his arms and legs spread helplessly, stood with his broad chest facing Dolokhov directly and looked at him with sorrow. Denisov, Rostov, and Nesvitski squeezed their eyes shut. At that same instant they heard a shot and Dolokhov's furious cry.
"Missed!" Dolokhov shouted, and he lay helplessly face down in the snow.
Pierre clutched his temples and, turning around, walked into the forest, trampling through the deep snow and muttering incoherent words:
"Madness... madness! Death... lies..." he repeated, his face contorted.
Nesvitski stopped him and took him home.
Rostov and Denisov drove away with the wounded Dolokhov.

Dolokhov lay silent in the sleigh with his eyes closed, not answering any of the questions put to him. But as they entered Moscow he suddenly came to and, lifting his head with effort, took hold of Rostov's hand — Rostov was sitting beside him. Rostov was struck by the completely altered, unexpectedly tender and emotional expression on Dolokhov's face.
"Well? How do you feel?" he asked.

"Bad! But that's not it, my friend —" said Dolokhov in a gasping voice. "Where are we? In Moscow, I know. I don't matter, but I've killed her, killed... She won't recover from this! She won't survive...."
"Who?" asked Rostov.
"My mother! My mother, my angel, my beloved angel mother," and Dolokhov squeezed Rostov's hand and burst into tears.
When he had calmed down a little, he explained to Rostov that he was living with his mother, who, if she saw him dying, would not survive it. He begged Rostov to go ahead and prepare her.

Rostov went on ahead to do as asked, and to his great surprise learned that Dolokhov the brawler, Dolokhov the bully, lived in Moscow with an elderly mother and a hunchbacked sister, and was the most devoted of sons and brothers.
